lastText: ☰⚙File ClosedA Record Argued For, Not AssumedMinor DefeatItalian High Command, 1939–1945End of hostilities: MAY 2, 1945 · filed out of sequence, pages missingImmediate AftermathArmy Group C surrenders in Italy on May 2, 1945, five days before the wider European war ends: the close of nineteen months fighting as a junior Allied partner on Italian soil. The human cost of this path runs higher than the historical one at nearly every hinge point: Italy's own wartime dead, roughly 300,000 military and civilian combined split across two governments and a country fought over twice, were already among the higher tolls of any Axis power relative to population. Mussolini's answer to Romania was delayed rather than rushed: the single change every honest account of the Greek campaign says should have been made, and on this path, was. The delay meant to buy Rome a coordinated defense instead bought German intelligence two additional days to reinforce the garrison: Operation Achse executed even more completely than its historical version. Cremona crossed the Senio at Alfonsine on April 10, 1945 and went on to Venice; Friuli entered Bologna on the 21st beside the Poles; the Nembo's second battalion drove off the German 1st Parachute Division five times at Case Grizzano. No branch of this campaign avoids the armistice fork; the war that follows it was already decided by an arithmetic no single command, on either side of the line, could overturn.One Year LaterA year past Army Group C's surren
